utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The witness is not yet in the courtroom. I do understand that the issue of a reservation to the 92 ter statements of Mr. Liborius are not there anymore. Is that correct, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's correct, but we did indeed discuss with the Gotovina Defence last night the issue of the admissibility under Rule 92 ter and we also got some feedback from the Cermak Defence. I understand that the Gotovina Defence agrees with us that their concerns that were raised in connection to Rule 91 have nothing to do with the formal admissibility of the statements under Rule 92 ter. Of course, the introduction of the 92 ter statements is no acknowledgment by the Defence even if they haven't objected to the 92 ter statement as to the contents of the statement. They can fully cross-examine, of course, the witness on these statements. It is simply an acknowledgment, we believe, that the procedural requirements have been met of Rule 92 ter. So I would like to renew my written and oral application to have these five witness statements entered at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I hear from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think in fairness to the witness it might be wise to do this in private session, my portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Just to inform the public that after having heard further arguments on the admissibility of witness statements given by the present witness, Mr. Liborius, the Chamber decided that the statements given by the witness on the 2nd of November, 1995; the 11th of November, 1997; the 12th of October, 2005; the 20th of June, 2008; and the 5th and 6th of September, 2008, are admitted into evidence under the respective numbers, same order, P799 up to and including P803. Are you ready to continue your examination-in-chief, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, could I ask you to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Liborius. Before we proceed, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Waespi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We left off yesterday about your findings in relation to that crater analysis you did outside the ECMM office or your accommodation. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I conducted a total of four crater analyses, two and two, in the days after Operation Storm when we had a chance to revisit the RC centre and our accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you note your findings in any of the reports you had to draft?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not note the crater analysis in details because the reporting format, the RC Knin, the Regional Centre Knin, and I were supposed to edit, had the task of describing in general detail -- in general state, the general state of affairs. The RC Knin situation report and daily report were not really the -- the medium through which you would transmit such individual findings. But they were an underlying factor in our overall assessment, I should stress.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's turn to one of these overall assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this is 65 ter 5415. That's a report dated the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recognise this report? Mr. Liborius --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I cannot see the bottom of the report, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could scroll down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, it's dated 4th of August, shortly before midnight. And you make an assessment, since you're the author, under 1 and I read it out: "Since the all-out Croatian attack began 0500 this morning, the destructive effect to the RSK is both military and psychological devastating." Did you write this assessment?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you explain what you meant by the psychological devastating effect?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of day one, 4 August, it was my impression, based on our observations and our information from -- from the rest of the ECMM that by that time a significant breakdown of RSK structures had taken place and that was not only military but also psychological in the sense that there was a -- a collapse of the will to defend the territory. There was a lack of key personnel. There was an evacuation in progress. And there was a mood of -- of collapse.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when you wrote this, did you have in mind what the effect of the shelling was on the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had by the end of day one, experienced a shelling campaign that began quite intense at 5.00 in the morning, and it had various intensity throughout the day. It peaked in the morning hours and then moved into a more steady-state bombardment where the fire, at least what I could observe and hear and see, targeted different areas of the Knin town, and that, to me, indicated that no specific military target or no specific target was selected for -- for all the fire and by spreading the fire over a larger area in which the civilian population is still in, then you -- you gain the effect of -- of panic. That's a standard reaction when indiscriminate fire is employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you also observe shelling on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard shelling and I did observe some. It was of a considerable less intensity, as opposed to the -- throughout the 4 August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this current proposed exhibit could be tendered into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P804.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P804 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In one of your witness statements, I think it is in your first one, which is now P799, you characterize what you just described as indiscriminate fire, also as harassment fire. Do you want to add something as to the description you gave?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday I think that on answering one of your questions erroneously that could have been the interpretation that I only saw a few impacts in -- in the area of the RC and my accommodation. Let me be very clear: The number of impacts I saw in the area of the RC Knin building, the accommodation, and a little bit further down south where we also had monitors living in the direction down to Tvik factory, accommodation for workers, I saw many, many impacts. The impacts mainly are of artillery, heavy artillery. I had observed the sound of multiple rocket launchers. They are a bit more difficult to pinpoint than the impact of an artillery shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you form an opinion at the time about the quality of intelligence the Croatian army had?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. He is asking for an opinion. I don't know what basis this witness would form an opinion on Croatian intelligence capabilities. There'd been no foundation laid.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was, of course, a factual question, whether he did form an opinion. Then of course the next question would be on what that opinion would be based and there I think the Chamber would not be assisted by just hearing the opinion. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And it's part of page 4 in P799 where the witness gave his comment about that. But I can elicit it live.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, based on the observations you had made about the impact of artillery, at that time did it cross your mind what the intelligence of the Croatian artillery must have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, I don't think a foundation has been laid for this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can ask him as soon as he says "yes" what -- Mr. President has said what the basis was for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course it doesn't make sense to ask him about an opinion he never formed. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that's true. At the same time, the last question, however, was phrased differently. Did it cross your mind what the intelligence must have been. That's seeking a conclusion, because not what it was, but what --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what it must have been. Now, perhaps you must have an idea, Mr. Waespi, on what you need to form an opinion on what should have been there, so if would you start with that, and then we'll see if there's a sufficient basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know how good the Croatian intelligence was when they shelled the impacts you had observed?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian intelligence was in general --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is what I was afraid. I mean, he is not answering yes or no, he is going into what the opinion is. So, again, I would ask for a foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from that, Mr. Waespi, there's an implicit assumption that intelligence, when they shelled the impacts you had observed, we have heard from the witness that he has seen impacts. I think it has not been further explored. The specific impacts he was talking about where they came from. Try to -- let's try to see what the witness knows for a fact. One more chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the Croatian intelligence?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how do you know anything about Croatian intelligence?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my previous occupation, I had a chance to -- to get acquainted with Croatian intelligence prior to my deployment. In the area, I had a chance to talk with Croatian army officers, both before and after the Operation Storm. The knowledge was coinciding, in the sense that the Croatian intelligence picture corresponded very much to the picture the ECMM and the UN possessed. And I also know that a couple of countries own intelligence -- the intelligence picture was established by the fact that the conflict had gone on for many years and that a number of delegations, journalists and so on, had visited RSK area. After Operation Storm, I had a chance to speak with Croatian army personnel who, to me, described in considerable detail what went on in Knin on the 3rd and 4th of August, details that I would imagine would be difficult to have, unless you possessed a quite detailed picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt but this whole explanation is completely speculative. "I would imagine that would be difficult to have ..." I mean, how much more speculative can we get?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether that's speculation or whether that is forming opinion, Mr. Waespi, the witness is telling us in -- with a very rough brush he is creating a picture. It would certainly assist if we would have a more precise brush, talking about persons I have spoken to might be further explored as who they were, what their positions were, when discussions took place, what they told the witness so as to see whether we have -- coming closer to the picture whether we have the details and not just a very rough outline of the picture. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you identify one person you have talked about from the Croatian side, which gave rise to your comment about their level of knowledge, about --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked with persons, personnel of the 4 Guards Brigade. I don't have the name available now. But they were soldiers that I frequently talked with in my duty after Operation Storm. Prior to Operation Storm, I had the chance to speak with Croatian officials - I'm sorry I don't have the name now - in my preparation for the deployment to Knin. They were based in Zagreb. They were working in one of the newspaper agencies and in an agency dealing with refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Does that suffice, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It leaves more questions open than it answers. For example, talking about an official who works in a newspaper agency, that requires to know better what an official is and how this person gained his knowledge he shared with the witness. That's just one of the issues. Again, the rough brush might not be of great assistance. Could you tell us, an official working at the newspaper agency was he government employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The official working was in the office dealing with refugees and displaced persons in the Gracac area and in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And is that the same person as the person you referred to as working in the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we're talking about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two different persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- two different persons. Now, if you would tell us in detail what the one told you and when he told that you and whether you know what the basis of his knowledge was. Let's start with the official.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The official working with refugees and displaced persons issues I met first in Gracac and I later met the person in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you meet him for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the first time I met him in 1994, in the summer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Summer of 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Secondly, I met him in Zagreb in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In July, before my deployment to Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi, perhaps you further explore because, of course, I'm not examining the witness, but I just gave a brief example on what, at least, I would expect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You also said you met somebody from the Croatian military.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember what his position was within the Croatian military?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you're now moving to another source. I gave a few questions on the first source but not to exhaust because we still don't know exactly what that source told the witness. The person you met first in Gracac in 1994 then you later met in Zagreb, before being deployed, what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me the assessment of the RSK, so to speak, defence potential, the state of the economy, the mood of the population, the mood of the armed forces, the -- the way the defence was structured. I had the sense that, as he was working with refugee and displaced persons, of course, they form a good source of intelligence, that he was indeed a very knowledgeable person. What struck me was that once inside Krajina, I had been inside Krajina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take it step by step. You told us that the Croatian intelligence was good.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Coinciding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, intelligence -- this person which apparently worked with refugees, do you know whether he shared his -- what he learned from these refugees with other institutions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Institutions in the Croatian system?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For example, or with whomever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would with an almost 100 percent certainty believe that he was not only wanting to share but he was under an obligation to share it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now did he tell that you he did share it with anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. But that was quite common at that time. I guess most personnel engaged also in the Croatian intelligence would not tell a foreigner like me that -- that part of their work fed into an intelligence system but I think that is beyond any doubt established that all -- all such work is feeding into intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in respect, therefore, of this source of yours, apparently you formed an opinion that he fed the intelligence services with his information on the basis of what such a person's duty would have been and what you would have expect him to do and that makes you almost 100 per cent certain that this is what happened. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, would you please, when exploring other sources for the witness's opinion about intelligence, also seek details which give us a clear picture of -- on what the percentage of certainty of the witness is based on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to add to that - I don't know if we're talking about the same thing - but some foundation as to how this witness is qualified to assess intelligence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he told us how he assessed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there should be some foundation. He is now giving us how intelligence works and things like that. I don't think there's been anything in the statements to establish his background to make assessments of intelligence capabilities and processes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave that to Mr. Waespi at this time. But it certainly would add to the information for the Chamber to properly evaluate the testimony of this witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President. Your Honour, I'm sorry. Just to add to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a statement that said something to the effect that part of their work led into a system of intelligence that fed into something. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I gave guidance to Mr. Waespi up to a level more than usual. Let's not try to -- to give, all of us, more instructions to Mr. Waespi than I have already done. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to move on to a different subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to move to the aspect of looting and there are numerous references in your daily reports, also in your witness statement. And the first one is in your statement which is now P799. When you say - and this is recorded on page 4 at the bottom: "On the 5th of August from around noon time, Knin was in HV control and armoured units from the 7th Puma Brigade dominated the town. From my observation point, or post, I observed how the looting by these soldiers began instantly." Now, what's the basis for saying that in your witness statement?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis is that from my observation post in the UN Sector South headquarters I observed the transportation of private valuables from houses - TV sets, small appliances - being transported to a collection point just outside the gates of the UN Sector South, trucks constantly coming, offloading goods, private cars bearing the RSK number plates being parked in -- in huge rows. Soldiers obviously proud of their loot coming to -- to -- to exchange that for other stuff. It went on in front of our eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how do you know they were from the Puma Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tactical sign, insignias, on both the uniforms and the cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In your 2005 witness statement, which is now P801, you say that you could see HV trucks leaving the areas. Do you remember that instance, that you saw HV trucks leaving the area?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just have the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. It is page 3 in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps for ease of reference, the witness could be given the five witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be very practical. Madam Usher, could you please assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's on page 3 of the 2005 statement. Sorry -- yes, 2005.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not sure you're looking at the 2005 statement.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's the third statement in your bundle, dated 11 and 12 October 2005. On page 3, the seventh paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Again, if you could let the Chamber know whether you remember what you recorded here, and when it was and where it was that you saw that.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I referred to, that in front of the UN barracks HV trucks, we observed throughout the day, would come and unload the goods, return empty, and then come back with -- with new things. There was a constant traffic of soldiers and it apparently was some sort of a depot where all sorts of goods were brought in. In the beginning, light goods that you could carry; later on, heavier goods, and as I said, also cars that during some instances were used for -- for small racing games among the soldiers on -- on the parking space.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who loaded and unloaded these trucks?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was soldiers in -- from the -- from the HV, and there was a mix of -- of different soldiers. So it was, to my mind at that point, not one particular unit, one particular corps, so it gained into a party place where soldiers would rally and inspect the loot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, moving to another instance of looting you had observed by the 7th Puma Brigade. That was on the 7th of August, and I think it concerns the ECMM headquarters. Do you remember that you saw, again, the Puma Brigade being involved in -- in looting. And I can refer you to your first witness statement, which is P799, the last page. The middle of the top paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: "Approximately 1205 hours, three HV soldiers riding a civilian small Fiat car without registration plates arrived. They wore 7th Puma Brigade insignia." Do you remember this incident?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I very well do. I was out to recover my personal belongings in my accommodation, the one I described yesterday as the way I observed the first shelling at 5.00 in the morning. And the soldiers had apparently the intent of -- well, not apparently, they had the intent of emptying the houses of valuables they could carry away and I was in my own living-room collecting my own stuff, and they were quite surprised to see that somebody was indeed in the house. And they explained to me that it was their right to take what was of value in the house and I politely said, "You can't do that. It's my stuff." And it was a quite bizarre incident where soldiers very obviously surprised to see that -- that somebody is actually in the house, and luckily, the situation did not develop violently. But I told them that it was not possible for them just to start stealing my stuff or the stuff of the family. They had left a flat days before. But that was indeed a quite remarkable incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I see that you describe these HV soldiers as arriving in "a civilian small Fiat car without registration plates." Now was that the only time in the aftermath of Operation Storm that you saw HV soldiers in private vehicles without licence plates or did you observe other instances?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did observe that on a number of occasions. The use of cars without number plates in the days and weeks after Operation Storm was certainly not something special. If you had a car you would just ride in it. And number plates missing, to me, indicated that it was a car that was taken from an abandoned car, for example, having RSK licence plates before Operation Storm. Otherwise, it would have a Croatian licence plate, in most instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move on to next exhibit. That is 65 ter 4023 and this is a report of 7 August. And I direct your attention to the description of the general situation that: "Knin is now calm with soldiers from the 4th and 7th Brigade still carrying out small-scale looting and then ROM still applies for some teams but seems to be lifted for RC Knin." Now, I note that the author is Rick Bigland and you, yourself. Can you tell us who Rick Bigland was?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rick Bigland was my fellow operations officer in the Regional Centre Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my question again: How do you know that it was soldiers from the 4th and 7th Brigade who were carrying out this looting?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite simple. When soldiers are moving in vehicles with TAC signs and they, on their uniform, wore TAC signs, that is a clear identificator. And there is no reason why Croatian soldiers should suddenly swap uniforms in the days after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go to the second page of this exhibit, and to paragraph 5. "Economical, industrial and infrastructure matters," and letter b has the following comment: "In the Knin area it seems as if random looting and destruction of houses and property is about to reach a degree where it will get even more difficult to restart normal life here. Comment: It is very unlikely that this is a deliberate policy of the authorities. It is more likely that, as the front-line, more disciplined troops are moving out, the second-line soldiers are less disciplined and more ready to grab what they can. End comment." Do you remember whether it was you or Mr. Bigland who drafted this comment?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Mr. Bigland who drafted that comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you signed the -- the report yourself or co-authored together with Bigland. Is it consistent with what your assessment was at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The question is: Is his assessment consistent with his own assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No. Is Mr. Liborius' assessment consistent with the comment I just read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Assessment when, today or when he wrote the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: At that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I think we have established that he is the co-author of this report, so I don't see how he is asking him to -- whether his report is consistent with his own assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not necessarily -- if you're a co-author of a report, it could be that not -- your private assessment is fully reflected in that report. So therefore, the question is admissible. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We heard from you that it was Mr. Bigland who had drafted this part of the comment, so my question to you: At that time, according to your own observations is what is written here consistent with your observations at that time?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. On the 7th -- 7th of August, I think that I was at least disturbed by the activities, the looting that went on, clearly without any attempt to -- to control it, or to stop it. And indeed as you say, Your Honour, it was a co-authored report and the production procedure into a RC Knin daily report was so that different elements would be written throughout the day, and there was not a time to do a consolidated big discussion where everybody could be in full alignment with the comments. But that was Richard Bigland's words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On this note, can you tell us how these reports were drafted and finalised. Who would show -- or would somebody show you this report before it went out?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The drafting of the RC Knin reports was done in the following way. Information from the Regional Centre subordinated teams and coordination centres, the information gained by the Regional Centre staff itself, was then, as in -- in most reports in -- in hierarchical structures, compiled and with a -- with an eye to brevity, of course. They were edited and sent. Usually the person, the operations officer having the final responsibility for the editing would be the one sending it. And that was a task that rotated, rotated through the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in relation to this report, who would be the officer who had the final responsibility for the editing?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine that particular report would Rick Bigland had the last hands on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it could be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P805.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P805 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we move on to the next report, similar report. 4030, a report of the 8th of August, 1995. And, again, Mr. Bigland and Mr. Liborius as the co-authors.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On -- in paragraph 1 it talks about looting and vandalism that is ongoing. In paragraph 3, military matters, it mentions that the 4th Brigade will have a permanent stationing in north barracks in Knin. Do you know more about that, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Guards Brigade established itself with the garrisons that previously were used by the army of the RSK in the barracks that are located in the centre of town. And quite soon after Operation Storm, it became a usual barracks with traffic in and out, with soldiers being accommodated there, with all the life -- the military life that is associated with an active army barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, moving on to the last subparagraph, c, on the bottom of this page. It says: "HRC today had a meeting with the new military governor of Knin, General Cermak. ECMM was promised that FOM will be extended as quickly as possible, and in a few days in all areas on the main roads, other roads being used at your own risk." Now, who is the HRC, the first word in -- after letter c?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HRC is an abbreviation for Head of Regional Centre, the commander of the Regional Centre Knin, ECMM Regional Centre, at that time it was Colonel Philippe Augarde.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And were you present at this meeting with General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you know when it says that FOM, I guess that is freedom of movement, will be extended as quickly as possible, whether, at that time, on the 8th of August, 1995, freedom of movement was restricted for ECMM?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Freedom of movement was indeed restricted. The teams under the RC Knin were unable to exercise the usual road patrolling and we ourselves in the RC could move limited inside Knin but not to the full extent. And that was the subject of -- one of the subjects that was raised with General Cermak, because ECMM did enjoy the guarantees of freedom of movement from the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to the last page of this document, third page under item 6 b. The meeting with General Cermak is picked up. Let me read it. "In his meeting with General Cermak, HRC was told that a policija guard would be put on our former office building and that we would be able to use it again if required. The General apologised for the looting. Comment: Does that mean he will get my Rolex back?" Do you know who drafted this part of the comment -- or this part of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was drafted by Rick Bigland.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he -- he had an Rolex or at least a fake Rolex. I don't wear Rolex.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P806.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P806 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next report is 4040, Mr. President, and this is a daily report of the 9th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you address for the first time in the general situation, the situation outside Knin. Second sentence: "Looting and burning of the surrounding villages continues in plain view of UN and IOS." What are IOS, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the abbreviation for International Organisations, among them, of course, also ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What is the basis for this assessment by you? You feature as the sole author of this document.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis is the ECMM teams information, and by the 9th of August, we were slowly able to expand our usual monitoring and road patrolling activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in the third paragraph, military matters. There is, in line 4, a reference to the presence of a fairly well-known dirty group belonging to the Diverzantia who have a skull as their signal and that they belong to the 7th Brigade, wore normal Croatian camouflage uniform and weapons. And you go on to say that: "They cannot be described as irregular elements or terrorists." And they were observed in a village burning houses. What's the basis for this written observation, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my own observation, together with one of the RC Knin teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were many observations in what Mr. Waespi read out, and I think they should be broken down as to which specific observation he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can address that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see the members or units of this Diverzantia group?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them in the village of Biskupija as we entered the village. And as the roads were quite narrow, we passed each other from each end of the village, so close that you could reach out for the other car on the other side of the road. So we had to slow down and the group were apparently surprised to see us. They also slowed down. We observed them in the middle of the burning of the village, observed the tactical signs on the vehicles, observed the tactical signs on their uniforms, observed the -- the weapons they were wearing, bringing along, the burning of the houses that took place while we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how far were you away when you observed the burning of houses by these troops?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The closest house set on fire was -- well, the distance to the door there, I would say. 12, 15 metres or so. But the entire village was being searched, and houses were being set on fire there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, incidentally, did you ever hear of the presence of warlords in the aftermath of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not hear that, and it was not an issue. Warlords, if we define that as -- as commanders of -- of groups of persons who are somehow outside the formal chain of command, it was not an issue. The Croatian soldiers in general, they were in a military structure, they were under command, and the chain of command functioned. It was not an issue at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me turn to one sentence in your comment: "Beyond any doubt this is a war crime act," and I'm reading from the bottom of the first page. "The systematic burning of property, houses, stables, haystacks and the like. Depriving the population the possibilities of surviving in the area." Can you elaborate on -- on this comment, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The comment is my description of the information that the ECMM teams had produced and that pointed to the quite serious destruction of property, as I say, property, houses, stables, haystacks and the like. So it was the scale of the activity that was important to me. The systematic approach that it had in our observations at that time, and by war crimes, I would say that the removal of the material basis of life for civilians in the area, to my mind and to my training prior to that, would constitute a war crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we move on to the next page, paragraph 4, humanitarian and human rights. You report here or you note the small-scale looting and burning of houses in Drnis and then you go on to say and I quote: "However, they saw four Orthodox churches in a few villages, Zvjerinaca, Kosovo, Jovici, and Bujici, which had been completely untouched. Two of which had signs persuading people to stay away. These will be checked every couple of days to keep an eye on them. Comment: It appears that the Croat authorities may be being very clever protecting these Serb churches as they know there would be a huge outcry if they were seen to be abusing them." Do you recall who observed these churches and the way they stayed intact?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, myself, observe a couple of them and I did also in my routine patrolling in the weeks that followed Operation Storm pay attention to also religious sites, churches and graveyards. And it was my impression that they were untouched. I talked with soldiers on guard at the gate of graveyards and churches, asked them if I could see the church, what their brief was, what their instruction was, and I was told that they were specifically guarding those religious sites under the instruction of General Gotovina. And of course that is very good, that you do not burn churches and graveyards, destroy them. However, I would say that the same care should be also extended to the rest of the property.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When you say you talked to soldiers on guard, was that at that time you made those observations which are noted down here?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did talk with soldiers throughout the -- the -- the weeks. I made it a point, as all good monitoring activities should do, to gain as much firsthand information as possible. That includes talking with the soldiers on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the reference to "them telling you that they were specifically guarding those religious sites under the instruction of General Gotovina." Do you remember who told you that and when and where?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that the monastery that is to the south-west of Knin, Krka -- one of the monasteries -- if I'm issued a card, I can find it. And also the guard at the Kosovo Polje church. And both gave identical information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, could I seek clarification from your previous answer. The question was: Do you remember who told you? Now, the first part of your answer is: "I was told that the monastery that is to the south-west of Knin," where you say you don't -- it's one of the monasteries. If I'm issued a card you could find that, and then you said: "And also the guard at Kosovo Polje church." But I have not heard in the first portion of your answer who told you apparently something about this monastery.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was a guard. I believe that I should speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- a guard at the monastery which could you find on the map and also a guard at the Kosovo Polje church.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The monastery I'm referring to is the monastery that is located to the south-west of Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not seeking these details. I was just trying to understand where the second person was in your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Guards both places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Army guards in regular Croatian army uniform with their weapon and standard soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you recall when it was that you got this information from them?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was fairly recent after we were out doing road patrolling again. If I'm given a chance to burrow through the ECMM reports, I can find it. But fairly soon after.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how do you talk to these soldiers? In what language?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either I would be talking through my interpreter or I would be talking to them myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in what language would you talk to them, without an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would talk Serbo-Croatian or German, a little English here and there. It was possible to be carrying out a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that would be admitted, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P807.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P807 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Next proposed exhibit, Mr. President, is 65 ter 5416. This is a report, ECMM report, dated the 12th August, and I'd like to go to political matters, the second numerated paragraph. And I quote: "General freedom of movement is still the rule. However, a number of patrols from UN and ECMM have been restricted locally with reference to safety reasons. This concern for safety does not apply to the civilian Croats passing through the same areas." Now, Mr. Liborius, do you remember this observation?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I observed it myself many times and so did the -- the teams in RC Knin. The situation would usually be that the team would be stopped at a check-point by either Croatian civilian police or military police without permission to enter, it could be a hamlet or a village or a wooden area or any other specified area, and often the reason would be given that there was danger ahead. There would be either RSK soldiers, there would be de-mining, there would be something that constituted a type of military threat that you could not really argue against. And of course we observed that. At the same time, however, unless you would be waiting at a check-point like that you would frequently see Croatian civilian cars passing by in both directions in and out of that particular area. And sometimes when I addressed the check-point commander, whether the same safety precautions wouldn't also apply to the civilian Croats I was given a smile or -- or a non-answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move to paragraph 3, smaller letter e, and here there is reference to teams Knin, and another UN patrol that were stopped from patrolling in the Vrlika area. They were escorted away. And there is a comment, and I quote: "It seems clear that the HV in the Vrlika area are trying desperately to hide something, maybe the continuing burning of houses between Drnis and Vrlika, lots of which were seen during the night drive back to Knin or maybe some more terrible abuses of human rights. It will be discovered eventually." Do you remember this instance, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just read it here. I have not experienced that myself. It would be the personnel of -- of -- as it's said November 2 and 3, together with the Head of Regional Centre. I am the operations officer compiling that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have any doubts as to the accuracy of what was reported to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can lay a foundation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the objection is denied because whether the witness has any doubt is, of course, his personal observation whether he had any doubts. Of course without knowing on what such doubt would be based or on what belief in what was said is based, without that information, of course, it's not of great assistance to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you let us know what the reporting system was in relation to reports coming in and you putting it down on paper.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reporting system in the RC Knin, as in all ECMM, would be that the teams would produce their daily reports, and they would forward them to the Regional Centre, where the operations officer would compile them and fit them into the reporting format, and as I said before, with -- with due attention to -- to brevity and significance, then they would send it as the RC report. Now, with regard to -- to this particular information, there's also always the rule that you should be able to trace the information here and -- and either it's the RC staff, this is the case, Head of Regional Centre, and it is the November 2 and November 3 teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And remind us again of HRC?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Head of Regional Centre was Colonel Philippe Augarde at that time. And I could honestly see no reason why I should doubt the factual information contained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I move that into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objection. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P808.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P808 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next proposed exhibit is 4381.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this is a report authored by you, Mr. Liborius, on the 18th of August, 1995. And I'm interested in --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can we scroll up to the top, please. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm interested in the second paragraph, freedom of movement, ROM. What does ROM mean, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Restriction of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I quote: "At one occasion, N2 was denied access to an area. However, a phone call to General Cermak solved the problem. See below." And we can actually move to the second page, subparagraph (c), security and FOM. And I quote: "Having waited two minutes at the combined Croatian MUP, MP CP in Dabar and being told not to move, N2 phoned General Cermak (see N2 DR yesterday) requesting him to solve the problem of FOM. This solved the problem and after a few minutes, N2 was back in business. Comment: There is still a problem with the flow of information in the Croatian chain of command. When two authorities, the military and civilian police are involved, the problem magnifies. Advice: Don't hesitate to call the supreme chiefs in the area." Do you know how it came about that N2 was able to call General Cermak directly?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were issued by the General himself the phone number. It also happened in a meeting he held with me, and he advised us to call him if we encountered restrictions of movement and then he would address the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you personally, how often did you use the phone connection to General Cermak, in order to get something done; for instance, past a check-point?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that frequently. As soon as I encountered restriction of movement I would wait, as it said there, a very short time, before following that agreement and call him. If not he, then his aides would answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you always successful or was there an instance, that despite Mr. Cermak's or his aide's intervention you couldn't get through?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall a instance where we were not able to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And lastly on this document, the comment which is made here, and drafted by you, that: "When two authorities, the military and civilian police are involved, the problem magnifies." Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The check-points that were manned both by civilian police and military police, it was explained to us also by the Croatian army liaison officers that the military police exercised authority over military personnel that would be encountered at the check-point, and civilian police would exercise authority over civilians. Sometimes discussion - and that's what I'm referring to here - discussions would develop between the staff at the check-point who would be the most senior to take the decision, whether to allow our team to proceed or impose restriction of movement. And as that was frequently the case, the advice that is carried in that report was the Regional Centre's advice to the teams out in the field, to use the -- the phone number of the General Cermak or his aides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you would require, successfully now as we know, General Cermak's intervention whether the check-point was civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not make any difference. He -- as I said, I cannot remember any instance where such an intervention was not able to solve the problem, meaning us being able to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Just lastly on this document. Can you tell us what was N2? November 2?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: November 2, or N2, is the designator for the second team in RC Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how many teams were there in RC Knin?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The RC structure was adapted to the -- to the changing situation. At the time of the Operation Storm, the RC had directly subordinated to it November 1, November 2, November 3. It was able to dispatch from its own ranks a team inside Knin. It had a number of CC centres. It had a team in Dubrovnik, field monitoring in Split, CC Zadar. Sibenik. The change of name or location, change of name and location took place sometime after Operation Storm. The -- whenever you come across the November 1, November 2, November 3, or so, these are team designators.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to tender this exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if we can get clarification in light of the last answer, but is the witness part of N2? Is this something he eye-witnessed? I don't know that that was clear. And is he one of part of any of these three teams. Because it wasn't clear to me whether ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, can I answer -- I can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you explain your role vis-a-vis these patrols, these teams?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accompanied N2 and formed a part of the team when I was not on my operations officer duty. Later on, I was designated as the team leader of N2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to consult my notes or my diary. But it was ... if we asked for a specific date I prefer my notes or diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yeah, I think you might be able to use the break for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P809.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P809 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Waespi, I think we should first have a break. We resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, during the break did you have a chance to review your notes in order to find out when you became team leader of N2?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And the date was 18 August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you would please close your diary or your notes, and in case you need them, you can certainly ask Mr. President whether you're allowed to consult them. Let's move on to 65 ter 4117. Do you recognise this list, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you let Their Honours know what it is, what it depicts?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a response to an ECMM order issued 21st August to all teams to compile the information on at least a weekly basis with regard to burning and destruction of the -- the hamlets and villages in each team AOR. And this is a document where the sources of information is November 1, November 2, November 3, Gospic and Split, abbreviated N1, N2 and N3 GNS, and in it there is a compilation of assessments of individual villages, hamlets or other points mentioned in maps. The information is then whether the area, the hamlet, the village, the city, is not destroyed, limited destroyed, deserted, what is the status of the different locations. The purpose was to draw an assessment on the possibilities for people to go to the different hamlets or villages or places.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you let us know how many people being members of these sources, N1 to S, you listed participated in these patrols, in order to collect the data recorded?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be no less than 12 people. A team structure would usually be at least two persons, a driver; and in larger teams co-located you would have more staff to -- to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, there has been evidence in this courtroom that there was a study, a similar study done by the UNMOs. Did you work together with the UNMOs in doing this study or was it done independently?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This study is a -- an ECMM work. I should perhaps be very clear that the RC structure, of course, also helped in compiling this document. The 12 people would be only the monitors in the teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there a difference in the cars the UN, UNMOs, and ECMM had, which was recognizable for the locals?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. ECMM cars had their own specific look. UNMOs used other cars, their own markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So just to be clear, whatever was entered into this study came from your own ECMM-generated data and not from other data?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I would imagine, the sources N1, N2, N3 Gospic and Split, yes. It was a combined effort, so I was not the only one participating in the drafting of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who else was involved?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the staff of the -- the Regional Centre in the RC Knin. The Regional Centre Knin located the Regional Centre staff to Zadar on the 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would make an objection as to a non-responsive answer. I'm still not sure whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Liborius, there was a rather simple question which was whether data entered and used for this study exclusively were ECMM-generated data. Your answer is not clear. You said, as I would imagine, or involvement of others -- were there any data received from other agencies than ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say, I don't think so. Are you sure that they were exclusively ECMM-generated data? What makes you doubt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The standard procedure, when the report -- excuse me, for, Your Honour, for a little elaborated answer. The sources indicated would exclude UNMO information or others. Now, as I'm not the signing-off person of this document, I can only say that to the best of my belief. I don't know if that satisfies the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then add one question. You were a member of N2, if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Data provided by N2 for this report, were they exclusively data gathered and obtained by N2, as far as you were aware of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was no other input by anyone --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- else. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to move this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P810.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P810 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could move on to 65 ter 4116.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this is a daily report authored by you and Mr. Hendriks. Can you tell the Trial Chamber who Mr. Hendriks was or is?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks was my fellow monitor colleague in team November 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to go to page 2, humanitarian and human rights issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you can please read paragraphs a and b, which deals with observations made by N2. And you observed a HV MP car carrying two uniformed MP wearing 72nd BAT sign and a JNA light truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that it be specifically -- it is not JNA, it is INA, or I-N-A, which could be important.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember this incident, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did -- yes, I do. I did also take a picture of the development.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us a little bit more of what you observed?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On our patrol, we observed smoke coming from a remote village, remote in the sense that it was quite far away from the main road, and there was only one dirt track leading up to it, and we wanted to investigate further the events there. And we departed the main road, took the dirt track up to the hamlet, and we met the HV military police car - it was a BMW, if I'm not mistaken - and the INA truck just coming out of the -- the, so to speak, centre of the hamlet, and there was no other entrance to that hamlet. So we wanted to see whether there were any other movements, any other cars in that hamlet. There wasn't. And the -- my team observed the -- the fire as it took the -- the house and the stable and the haystack of a house at the -- at the south end of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the INA truck looked like?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The INA truck was a Mercedes van-type truck, white, with one of the blue stripes on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had INA signs on the -- on the van.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what does it carry?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: An INA truck would -- as INA company is the oil company, it would be a truck usually associated with delivery of petrol products.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And your assessment was who was responsible for setting light to these structures?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I write in the report, the circumstances surrounding the torching of houses and stables and haystacks in that area could, to my mind, only be done by these persons from the HV military police car and the INA light truck. We saw simply no other traces of persons in the -- in the village. We observed it for 40 minutes, and we got to the place just as the house had caught fire. The roof was still intact when we came to that part of the hamlet and we departed when the roof had collapsed and we patrolled the hamlet without finding anyone else. There was only one access route to that particular hamlet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, one of your previous answers when asked what this truck carried, you said that you would associate this truck with the delivery of oil products because it was an oil company. Could you also tell what the truck carried, if you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have any chance to inspect the truck, but it had the markings, it had the look of a truck that would usually carry petrol products.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was a truck -- covered, enclosed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a covered and closed truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I'd like to move to the comment in the same paragraph, just a few lines down. "The promises regarding property made by the Croatian leadership in general and General Cermak for the Knin region in particular, clearly has a hollow tone." Do you remember who made this comment?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The comments were made by various Croatian officials, including General Cermak. They were also made by the -- by the government in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. My question was -- I'm sorry, I wasn't clear enough. Who drafted this comment in this ECMM report?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me and Eric Hendriks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And going back to the comment attributed to the Croatian leadership and General Cermak, were you present when a comment was made by General Cermak to -- to that effect, or a promise, a promise was made by General Cermak as recorded in this report?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The promises were aired on radio, they were given in meetings. I heard them a couple of times both in radios and at meetings, public gatherings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And why do you write that these promises have a hollow tone?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the involvement of especially HV military police personnel, to me, indicates that the persons who should ensure safety and protection of property were in the middle of burning things down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P811.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P811 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to the next exhibit. This is it 4392, a report, daily report, dated 23rd August by Mr. Liborius and Mr. Hendriks. And I'd like to move to page 2. The top paragraph, small a, carries reference to an informal meeting with the commander of the HV forces stationed in B, and I believe B is defined on the first page as Benkovac. Do you know more about this commander of the HV forces? Have you met him?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please allow me time to read it here. Yes, I recognise that, yes. Yeah, I met him in the Benkovac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know what his unit was called?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to consult my notes. It was a regular army unit. He talked at length about having received his military training in the US, in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thanks. Let's move to the second alinja [phoen] b, and I quote: "During today's patrol following was observed. Kistanje, in the auto workshop by the INA station, a fire was lit at 11.04. Next to the place was seen one civilian bus with HV soldiers, registration number SI 253-AB; and a Renault car, SI 24 -- 254-S. As the fire was lit, soldiers embarked the bus and the cars left the scene." Do you know more about this instance, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my team observed the incident on patrol in Kistanje, and the bus, a standard size 50-person bus was -- with Croatian army soldiers stopped at this petrol station/workshop that was located in the centre of -- of Kistanje, and for reasons not clear to me, they -- they disembarked the bus and went to the workshop and station and -- and set it on fire, observed that the fire had caught good ground and then they -- they left again. And after that, we continued our patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You may not know that but let me ask you, do you know what SI in the registration number plates refers to?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Liborius. And lastly on this page, in this document, humanitarian and human rights issues, small paragraph a: "Given the statement by General Cermak two days ago about the 100 persons already having returned to Biskupija, N2 tried to pay these people a welcome-back visit. However, N2 cannot confirm the return of 100 persons." And at the end there's an assessment: "Maybe General Cermak was inflating the numbers of returned." Do you have any observations on this record?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We patrolled the area of Biskupija with a view to -- to try and find these persons. Biskupija is quite a well-defined village, and we were unable, as it is stated in the report, to find any of these persons. What we did find was a few houses on fire, and there's really not much more to add than saying that the statements that these persons could have returned we could not substantiate by our findings in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you allow me to ask one or more clarifications on the document. Mr. Liborius, on the second page, second line, it's described that there's been an informal meeting with -- in the B house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could we move up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, second page, second line -- well, third line, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I please see the first part of the report. Yes, please, scroll down. Yes, Your Honour, could I have your question, please again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reference is made on the second page, third line, about in the B house of the HV, which is not clear to me what that means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the Benkovac house of the HV, meaning the officers and NCOs' recreation facility next to the barracks. House of the army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They were accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question is second page, military situation under b, you are talking about the civilian bus with HV soldiers. Do you have any further details as to these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers wore all normal Croatian army uniforms. They were riding together in one bus. I saw different ranks among the soldiers. I would imagine that they constituted a normal military unit. Does that satisfy your question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should add that we were actually parked right opposite the auto workshop and the distance between the bus and my patrol vehicle was less than ten metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember approximately the number of soldiers who were boarding the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 20, 25, roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any objections against admission. No. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P812.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P812 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we move to 65 ter 4390.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is a daily report dated the 24th of August. And I'd like to go to the middle of the page, military situation, little a: "N2 went to Bosanski Grahovo, ten civilian buses, ten trucks, and 15 other vehicles were observed. Troops were resting in the town, receiving mail. The officers large envelopes, and new ribbons were being given to the units. The vehicles bore registration plates -- registration plated from HVO, HVO and Mostar, ZD and SI." Now, again, have you -- were you personally on that N2 patrol?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Bosanski Grahovo is where exactly?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosansko Grahovo is in Bosnia, as the name would indicate, and is located to the east of -- of Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the -- in the northern part of the -- of the adjacent Herzegovina area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And why would you go to -- to Bosnia? Was that part of your mandate?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ECMM mandate included all the six republics of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I object as to a non-responsive answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is yes, it was our mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then take it that your mandate was not split up to certain portions, that you would be assigned a task in a limited area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would be assigned a task in a limited area. However, depending on the situation that area would be flexible. For example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And your area included parts of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The adjacent areas of UN Sector South, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
